Learning Objectives
Explain the importance of risk-stratifying patients based on preexisting medical conditions,
and describe the manner in which these medical conditions relate to postoperative outcomes.
List indications for preoperative tests that may alter perioperative medical management and
intraoperative anesthetic management.
Discuss medical treatment options (pharmacologic and non-pharmacologic) that may reduce
the risk of postoperative complications.

All patients undergoing surgery and anesthesia are at risk for medical complications.
Orthopaedic surgeons should be aware of educational tools to aid in risk stratifying
patients based on age, comorbidities, and functional status. This is the first step in
weighing the risks and advantages of proceeding with surgery. The surgical risks (eg,
blood loss, embolism, etc.) to a patient also must be considered; however, those factors
are beyond this scope of this lesson. In addition, orthopaedic surgeons should
understand the importance of patient optimization, such as performing additional
medical tests, initiating new therapies preoperatively, or discontinuing current therapies
that may be associated with an increased risk of postoperative complications.
Cardiac Disease
Risk of Major Adverse Cardiac Event
The Revised Cardiac Risk Index (RCRI) is a simple and well-validated tool to estimate the risk of
perioperative major adverse cardiac events (MACE). In general, patients with a low risk of a
MACE (<1% as calculated using the RCRI) do not require additional cardiac tests
preoperatively.1-3

Risk of Major Adverse Cardiac Event
Performing a thorough patient evaluation involves assessment of patient-specific and
procedure-specific risk factors. The RCRI (Lee Index) is one of the simplest and most
widely used tools to estimate the risk of a MACE during the perioperative period. The
RCRI includes six equally weighted cardiovascular risk factors, each of which indicates an
increased risk of a major cardiac complication defined as cardiac death, nonfatal
myocardial infarction, nonfatal cardiac arrest, postoperative cardiogenic pulmonary
edema, and complete heart block1 (Figure 1; Table 1). The risk factors are listed in a
footnote in Table 1.

Evaluation of Functional Capacity
Patients who are unable to achieve 4 metabolic equivalents (METs) of workload require a
cardiac consultation and most likely will require a cardiac stress test preoperatively.2,4

Evaluation of Functional Capacity
Evaluation of a patient’s functional ability is essential in evaluating his or her
perioperative risk of cardiovascular complications. Functional capacity is expressed in
terms of METs, in which 1 MET is the basal oxygen consumption of a 40-year-old man
who weighs 70 kg. Perioperative risk is considerably increased in patients who are not
able to achieve more than 4 METs of workload. Common activities that can be used to
estimate functional capacity greater than 4 METs include walking up a flight of stairs,
walking on flat ground at a speed greater than 4 mph, and performing moderate
housework (eg, scrubbing floors, lifting/moving furniture). Another subjective, but useful
tool is a 12-part questionnaire called the Duke Activity Status Index (Table 2), which
better approximates functional ability.4 Determining functional capacity in terms of
METs is an indispensable component of the preoperative evaluation because it has a
direct effect on clinical decision making.

For emergent surgery, surgeons generally prefer to forego preoperative cardiac tests or
time-consuming medical optimization; however, most orthopaedic surgeries are elective
and, therefore, allow for medical optimization and perioperative risk reduction. Testing
beyond a thorough patient history and physical examination is necessary only in patients
with a high risk for cardiovascular events. The ACC/AHA provides a useful algorithm for
treating patients with known or suspected coronary artery disease who are undergoing
surgery (Figure 2). In general, if a patient can generate 4 METs of activity without
cardiopulmonary symptoms, then a stress test is not indicated; however, if a patient’s
estimated risk of a MACE is greater than 1% and his or her functional capacity is lower
than 4 METs or is unknown, then cardiovascular stress tests are warranted.

Perioperative Management
Recent Myocardial Infarction
Patients who have experienced a recent myocardial infarction (not requiring percutaneous
intervention) should be scheduled for elective orthopaedic surgery a minimum of 60 days after
the cardiac event.2,5

Recent Myocardial Infarction
A history of prior ischemic cardiac events is associated with a MACE after noncardiac
surgery. The temporal relationship between a prior coronary artery disease event and a
planned surgical procedure has tremendous effects on postoperative morbidity and
mortality. The ACC/AHA clinical practice guidelines recommend that, in the absence of
coronary intervention, at least 60 days should elapse after an myocardial infarction
before proceeding with noncardiac surgery.2 This recommendation is based on data
from a retrospective study of discharge summaries from patients who underwent hip
surgery, cholecystectomy, colectomy, elective abdominal aortic aneurysm repair, and
lower extremity amputation5 (Table 3).

Percutaneous Coronary Intervention
Surgery should be delayed a minimum of 30 days after bare metal stent placement and 6
months after drug-eluding stent placement.6

Percutaneous Coronary Intervention
After undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention for the management of coronary
artery disease, patients are placed on strict dual anti-platelet therapy (aspirin and a
P2Y12 inhibitor) for 1 to 12 months and low-dose aspirin indefinitely.6 Interruption of
dual anti-platelet therapy increases the risk of in-stent thrombosis and, therefore,
should be minimized and carefully weighed against the risk of bleeding from the planned
surgical procedure. According to the 2016 ACC/AHA guidelines, elective noncardiac
surgery should be delayed for 30 days or more after bare metal stent placement and a
minimum of 6 months after drug-eluting stent placement6 (Figure 3). Interruption of
dual anti-platelet therapy for elective noncardiac surgery should include temporary
cessation of P2Y12 inhibitors but continuation of low-dose aspirin therapy throughout
the perioperative period.

Valvular Heart Disease
All patients with valvular heart disease require an echocardiogram within 1 year of elective
surgery. If any symptomatic changes have been noted or changes are noted on physical
examination, the echocardiogram should be repeated.7

Valvular Heart Disease
Aortic stenosis is the most common valvular abnormality and the most common cause
of left ventricular outflow obstruction in adults. This obstruction to flow requires
increased workload from the left ventricle to maintain adequate cardiac output, which
results in left ventricular hypertrophy, reduced diastolic filling, and reduced
subendocardial blood flow. Combined, these factors increase the risk of myocardial
ischemia during general or neuraxial anesthesia. Aortic stenosis is an independent risk
factor for postoperative pneumonia, acute renal failure, and septicemia.7 In practice,
neuraxial anesthesia often is considered to be relatively contraindicated in patients with
severe aortic stenosis. This is based on the theoretic risks that rapid sympatholysis and
reduction in preload may induce a considerable or profound reduction in coronary
perfusion pressure, resulting in cardiac ischemia. However, prospective clinical trials
investigating this claim do not exist. Similarly, no prospective evidence has shown a
cardioprotective effect of neuraxial anesthesia compared with general anesthesia.
However, retrospective data support that spinal anesthesia may be safer than general
anesthesia in patients with aortic stenosis who are undergoing noncardiac surgery.8
Regardless, selecting general anesthesia versus neuraxial anesthesia for patients with
aortic stenosis remains controversial.

Heart Failure
Elective surgery should be deferred for at least 3 months after the initiation of goal-directed
medical therapy in patients with newly diagnosed heart failure. Surgery should be deferred in
patients with decompensated heart failure, if possible, until stabilization of heart failure
symptoms has been achieved according to goal-directed medical therapy.9

Heart Failure
The ACC/AHA defines heart failure as a “complex clinical syndrome that results from any
structural or functional impairment of ventricular filling or ejection of blood.” Heart
failure is broadly grouped into two categories with vastly different structural and
functional pathophysiologic mechanisms: heart failure with preserved ejection fraction
and heart failure with reduced ejection fraction. The current literature has not
established an obvious variation in the perioperative risks between these two
categories.2,9,10
Patients with symptomatic or decompensated heart failure have a considerably
increased risk of 30-day postoperative complications, whereas clinically stable heart
failure does not appear to be associated with the same risks.2,10 Therefore, elective and
nonurgent surgeries should be postponed until stabilization of heart failure symptoms
has been achieved using goal-directed medical therapy. Signs and symptoms of heart
failure include dyspnea at rest, dyspnea on exertion, paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea,
orthopnea, pulmonary rales, bilateral lower extremity edema, jugular venous distention,
and the presence of third heart sound. With regard to newly diagnosed heart failure, the
European Society of Cardiology/European Society of Anesthesiology guidelines
recommend that elective, intermediate, and high-risk noncardiac procedures be
deferred for at least 3 months after the initiation of medical therapy.9
Preoperative echocardiography should be strongly considered in patients with known or
suspected heart failure because it provides useful information on structural and
functional pathologies that may help guide perioperative management, such as
anesthetic techniques (general versus neuraxial), intraoperative monitoring techniques

(continuous blood pressure monitoring), and fluid management strategies. For urgent
surgery (eg, hip fractures), the risk of delaying surgery for cardiac consultation and
formal preoperative echocardiography may outweigh the advantages.11 A study that
examined focused transthoracic echocardiography performed by anesthetists in patients
at risk for cardiac disease who were undergoing hip fracture surgery reported a lower
30-day and 12-month mortality rate in the patients who underwent transthoracic
echocardiography. These data support that preoperative echocardiography in patients
with known or suspected heart disease provides useful information for guiding
perioperative management and may improve short- and long-term outcomes; however,
this decision should be carefully balanced against the risks of delaying urgent surgery.
Focused, point-of-care transthoracic echocardiography performed by a skilled
anesthesiologist may be the best treatment option in time-sensitive cases.

Respiratory and Pulmonary Disease
Asthma

Patients with asthma should be instructed to bring all inhalers with them to their scheduled
surgery. In general, chest radiographs, and blood gas analysis are not necessary
preoperatively.

Asthma
Asthma is a broad category of lung pathologies characterized by wheezing because of
bronchospasm, dyspnea, chest tightness, cough, variable expiratory airflow limitation,
and chronic airway inflammation. Severity of asthma is classified as intermittent,
persistent mild, persistent moderate, or persistent severe. Airway instrumentation can
trigger bronchoconstriction; therefore, all patients with asthma should be evaluated
carefully in the preoperative holding area. Medicated prophylaxis should be strongly
considered before undergoing general anesthesia because of the inherent superiority of
prevention over treatment in patients with asthma.
Preoperative evaluation of patients with known asthma should include inquiry of known
triggers, dyspnea, wheezing, cough (specifically nighttime), recent exacerbations, therapy
(specifically corticosteroids), prior hospitalizations (specifically to intensive care units and
those requiring endotracheal intubation), and recent upper respiratory tract infections.
Physical examination should include assessment of quality of breath sounds, the degree
of air movement, accessory muscle usage, and oxygen saturation. Although wheezing is
a common physical examination finding in patients with asthma exacerbation, the
intensity of wheezing tends to diminish as airflow obstruction worsens.
In general, preoperative chest radiographs are not necessary unless concern for
infectious etiology or pneumothorax exists. In general, blood gas analysis is not
necessary except in patients with severe exacerbation, usually accompanied by fatigue.
Inhaled B-adrenergic agonists (primarily albuterol and levalbuterol) are useful
prophylactic medications in the preoperative holding area; therefore, patients should
bring all inhalers with them to their scheduled surgery. Optimally, patients being treated
with oral corticosteroids should have their fasting blood glucose level assessed

preoperatively. Any patient being treated via long-term chronic steroid therapy may
require stress-dose steroids intraoperatively if refractory hypotension is noted.
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
Elective surgery should be delayed in patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
(COPD) exacerbation until baseline pulmonary function has been restored.12 Regional
anesthesia (peripheral nerve blocks or neuraxial anesthesia) has been demonstrated to
decrease postoperative pulmonary complications. Patients being treated via chronic
exogenous corticosteroid therapy should receive empiric stress-dose glucocorticoids before
the induction of anesthesia in accordance with the anticipated degree of surgical stress.

Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease
COPD shares many pathologic similarities with asthma; therefore, the preoperative
evaluation is similar, with specific emphasis on recent upper respiratory infections and
recent exacerbations. Preoperative clinical evaluation should focus on assessment of any
deviations from the patient’s baseline pulmonary status (eg, worsening dyspnea, change
in the quality or quantity of respiratory secretions, increased requirement of rescue
inhaler usage, or increased home oxygen requirement). If clinical assessment is unclear,
pulmonary function tests can be performed for additional evaluation. In general,
pulmonary function tests are not required in the routine preoperative evaluation of
patients with COPD, with the exception of patients undergoing lung resection.
In general, COPD medication regimens include inhaled beta-adrenergic agonists; inhaled
muscarinic antagonists; inhaled corticosteroids; and, in some patients, oral
corticosteroids, all of which should be continued throughout the perioperative period.
COPD is a well-established risk factor for postoperative pulmonary complications (eg,
atelectasis, pneumonia, acute respiratory distress syndrome, unplanned reintubation,
and bronchoconstriction).13,14 Preoperative optimization for current smokers should
include referral to a smoking cessation program, ideally 4 to 12 weeks preoperatively,
and inspiratory respiratory muscle training for at least 2 weeks preoperatively. A
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:34 PM
AAOS | Patient Optimization
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000594
13/34

standard inspiratory muscle training regimen includes five to seven supervised weekly
sessions, each of which is approximately 15 to 30 minutes. During the session, patients
inspire through an inspiratory threshold-loading device at a predetermined percentage
of their maximal inspiratory strength. A considerable reduction in postoperative
atelectasis, pneumonia, and hospital length of stay has been observed in adults who
undergo preoperative inspiratory muscle training before cardiac and major abdominal
surgery.12,15
Monitored anesthesia care, neuraxial anesthesia, peripheral nerve blocks, or a
combination of these techniques should be strongly considered in patients with COPD to
decrease the risk or intraoperative and postoperative pulmonary complications. A study
examined data from the National Surgical Quality Improvement Program reported
considerably lower rates of postoperative pneumonia, prolonged ventilator dependence,
and unplanned postoperative intubation in patients with COPD who received regional
anesthesia compared with those who received general anesthesia.16
Patients who are being treated via chronic corticosteroids therapy (more than 20 mg of
prednisone or its equivalent per day for more than 3 weeks during the previous 6
months) are assumed to have hypothalamic-pituitary-adrenal axis suppression and are
at risk for intraoperative adrenal insufficiency. Exogenous stress-dose corticosteroids
can be administered based on the anticipated degree of surgical stress. For minor
procedures, no additional exogenous corticosteroids need to be administered, and
patients should be advised to take their normal dose on the morning of surgery. For
moderate surgical stress (eg, total joint arthroplasty), 50 mg of hydrocortisone should be
administered intravenously immediately before the procedure, and 25 mg of
hydrocortisone should be administered every 8 hours for 24 hours. For major surgical
procedures (eg, total colectomy, open cardiac surgery), 100 mg of hydrocortisone should
be administered intravenously before the induction of general anesthesia, and 50 mg of
hydrocortisone should be administered every 8 hours for 24 hours.
Obstructive Sleep Apnea

9/3/26, 5:34 PM
AAOS | Patient Optimization

14/34

All patients who have been prescribed continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) for sleep
apnea should continue to use it postoperatively. Opioid medications should be minimized, and
multimodal approaches to pain management are encouraged. If opioid medications are
required, strict adherence to CPAP therapy is paramount, and admission for monitoring via
continuous pulse oximetry should be strongly considered.

Obstructive Sleep Apnea
OSA is characterized by the periodic collapse of the upper airway while sleeping,
resulting in hypopnea or apnea. Many patients have undiagnosed OSA preoperatively.
The prevalence of OSA is approximately 10% to 20% in the adult surgical population,
with as many as 80% of patients undiagnosed and untreated.17-19 Patients with OSA
pose anesthetic challenges with regard to airway management (mask ventilation, direct
laryngoscopy, endotracheal intubation, and fiberoptic visualization of the airway) and
have an increased risk of perioperative complications, such as prolonged intubation, risk
of reintubation, readmission after discharge, cardiorespiratory failure, hypoxic brain
injury, and death.
The preferred method for diagnosis of OSA is polysomnography, which measures the
number of apnea/hypopnea events per hour, called the apnea-hypopnea index. Because
of the time-consuming nature of this test, such assessment is impractical as part of a
routine preoperative workup for all patients in whom OSA is suspected. The STOP-Bang
Questionnaire is a simple and well-validated tool that can be used to screen for the
presence and severity of OSA (Table 5). For patients with an intermediate risk (score of 3
to 4), a baseline serum bicarbonate level greater than 28 mEq/L increases the specificity
of the STOP-Bang Questionnaire.20
In general, management of OSA involves CPAP, oral/mandibular appliances, weight loss,
or a combination of these techniques. Compliance with these therapies often is a
challenge for patients. Insufficient evidence is available to support the decision to cancel
or delay elective surgery to initiate positive airway pressure therapy in patients with a
high risk of OSA preoperatively; however, positive airway pressure therapy is

15/34

recommended for patients with considerable or uncontrolled systemic disease (eg,
hypoventilation syndromes, pulmonary hypertension, and resting hypoxemia).19,21
Preoperative identification of OSA is helpful in formulating a targeted management plan
to minimize postoperative complications. Important considerations include performing
surgery in an inpatient versus ambulatory setting, choice of anesthetic management
(general versus neuraxial), postoperative pain regimens, and close monitoring via
continuous pulse oximetry. A study of more than 30,000 patients with diagnosed sleep
apnea who underwent hip and knee arthroplasty revealed considerably lower rates of
major complications in patients who received neuraxial anesthesia compared with those
who received general anesthesia.18
The perioperative management of patients with uncontrolled or undiagnosed OSA is
highly variable between practitioners. Important considerations include comorbidities,
suspected severity of OSA, whether OSA is managed or unmanaged, compliance with
CPAP, patient health literacy and understanding of post-discharge instructions, risk level
of surgery, and anticipated intraoperative and postoperative opioid requirements. Open
communication between anesthesiology teams and surgery teams with regard to
discharge planning and anticipated levels of postoperative pain is strongly encouraged,
particularly in this patient population.

Chronic Kidney Disease
Chronic kidney disease is known to increase postoperative morbidity and mortality.22,23
Preoperative serum creatinine and electrolyte levels should be measured preoperatively in
patients with known or suspected chronic kidney disease.
Patients who have undergone renal transplantation should avoid interruption of
immunosuppressive medications.
Ideally, surgery should occur 24 hours after hemodialysis in patients with end-stage renal
disease. For patients being treated via peritoneal dialysis, the amount of dialysis should be
increased 1 week preoperatively with consultation from specialists.

Chronic Kidney Disease
Patients with end-stage renal disease have an increased risk of postoperative
complications, most likely attributable to a higher incidence of coronary artery disease,
increased fluid and electrolyte disturbances during the perioperative period (particularly
hyperkalemia), increased risks of bleeding complications, and poor blood pressure
control. Perioperative management should be centered around mitigation of these
physiologic abnormalities as much as possible. Baseline measurements of plasma
electrolyte levels (including phosphorus, magnesium, and calcium), glucose level, blood
urea nitrogen level, creatinine level, albumin level, and complete blood count via
coagulation studies should be obtained preoperatively.
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 5:34 PM
AAOS | Patient Optimization
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=510000594
17/34

Patients on hemodialysis should be dialyzed approximately 24 hours before elective
surgery with appropriately adjusted dialysate to target normal (or near-normal) plasma
electrolyte concentrations and near dry-weight. For patients on peritoneal dialysis, the
frequency of dialysis should be increased 1 week preoperatively in coordination with
specialists. Currently, no published evidence exists to support this strategy; however, it is
based on the anticipation that re-initiation of peritoneal dialysis can be delayed in the
immediate postoperative period (eg, ileus or constipation).
Diabetes Mellitus
A preoperative hemoglobin A1c level higher than 8.0% is associated with wound complications
in patients with diabetes mellitus undergoing total knee arthroplasty.24 Therefore, hemoglobin
A1c levels should be determined within 3 months preoperatively.
Intraoperatively and postoperatively, serum glucose levels should be between 80 and 180
mg/dL.25
Basal insulin coverage (eg, neutral protamine hagedorn, glargine, detemir, degludec) should
not be withheld during the perioperative period but may be decreased by 10% to 25% the
night before or the morning of surgery.
A combined basal-bolus treatment regimen is a more effective strategy than a sliding-scale
regular insulin regimen alone for patients with diabetes mellitus.
All oral medications should be withheld on the day of surgery, with the exception of sodium-
glucose co-transporter 2 inhibitors, which should be withheld 3 to 4 days preoperatively. In
general, these agents can be reinstated after the patient is alert and has resumed oral food
intake.

Diabetes Mellitus
Surgical stress produces a complex neurohormonal response, including the release of
counter-regulatory hormones, resulting in alterations in carbohydrate metabolism,
insulin resistance, increased hepatic glucose production, impaired peripheral glucose
use, and relative insulin deficiency. Each of these factors contribute to hyperglycemia,

which has been implicated in increased rates of infections, impaired wound healing, and
increased rates of acute coronary syndrome.26
Glycemic control in the perioperative period is highly variable because of numerous
individual factors, such as the duration of preoperative fasting, the degree of surgical
stress, anesthetic administration, perioperative emesis, the disruption of sleep-wake
cycles, the administration of intravenous fluids with dextrose, and the administration of
corticosteroids. Therefore, perioperative glycemic management is highly individualized
and may warrant a consultation with specialists.
The goals of the perioperative management of diabetes mellitus include avoidance of
hypoglycemia, avoidance of marked hyperglycemia, prevention of
ketoacidosis/hyperosmolar states, and maintenance of fluid and electrolyte balance.
Routine preoperative tests includes electrocardiography, serum creatinine level,
hemoglobin A1c level within 3 months, and current serum blood glucose concentration.
Although protocols vary across institutions, the American Diabetes Association
recommends initiating insulin therapy in most critically ill and noncritically ill patients
with a serum glucose concentration greater than or equal to 180 mg/dL.27 Bedside
glucose monitoring is recommended before meals in all patients with diabetes mellitus
and every 4 to 6 hours in patients with nothing-by-mouth status.
Insulin administration can be divided into three distinct categories: basal, prandial, and
corrective. All patients with insulin deficiency (type 1 diabetes mellitus and insulin-
deficient type 2 diabetes mellitus) must have basal insulin coverage at all times,
regardless of oral intake status. Therefore, basal insulin coverage (eg, neutral protamine
hagedorn, glargine, detemir, degludec) should not be withheld in the perioperative
period but may be decreased by 10% to 25% the night before or the morning of
surgery.28 However, prandial insulin (eg, regular, lispro, aspart, glulisine) should be
withheld while fasting. Corrective insulin (eg, regular, lispro, aspart, or glulisine) should
be administered if glucose measurements rise higher than 180 mg/dL according to
institutional protocols.

Although slightly more cumbersome, a combined basal-bolus treatment regimen is a
more effective strategy than a sliding-scale regular insulin) regimen alone in patients
with diabetes mellitus who are hospitalized. A randomized clinical trial comparing these
two strategies in insulin-naïve patients with type 2 diabetes mellitus who were
undergoing general surgery reported a considerable reduction between the groups with
regard to the frequency of the composite postoperative outcome, including wound
infection, pneumonia, bacteremia, respiratory failure, and acute renal failure.29
Oral diabetic medication regimens should be altered during the perioperative period to
decrease the risk of hypoglycemia while fasting. Sodium-glucose co-transporter 2
inhibitors (eg, empagliflozin, dapagliflozin, canagliflozin) should be discontinued 3 to 4
days preoperatively because of an increased risk of urinary tract infections, diabetic
ketoacidosis, and hypovolemia.25,30 Metformin should be withheld the morning of
surgery and reinstated after the patient is eating solid foods. However, reinstating
metformin therapy is contraindicated in patients with lactic acidosis, tissue hypoxia, and
renal hypoperfusion. Sulfonylureas (eg, glipizide, tolazamide, and glimepiride) should be
withheld the morning of surgery and should only be reinstated after baseline oral intake
has been confidently established because of the higher risk of hypoglycemia with these
particular agents. Initiating a reduced dose with up-titration is prudent. Similarly,
dipeptidyl peptidase-4 inhibitors (eg, sitagliptin, saxagliptin, linagliptin, and alogliptin)
should be withheld the morning of surgery but generally can be reinstated earlier in the
postoperative period because of a lower risk of hypoglycemia. Thiazolidinediones (eg,
pioglitazone and rosiglitazone) should be withheld the morning of surgery but should
not be reinstated in patients with congestive heart failure, fluid retention, or liver
function abnormalities.
Gastrointestinal and Liver Disease
Patients with moderate to severe liver disease should undergo a preoperative workup,
including electrocardiography, complete blood count, electrolyte concentration, creatinine
level, blood urea nitrogen level, prothrombin time/international normalized ratio, partial
thromboplastin time, fibrinogen level, albumin level, bilirubin level, and transaminase level
(alanine aminotransferase/aspartate transaminase).

Elective surgery is contraindicated in patients with acute or fulminant liver disease. These
patients have a very high risk of morbidity, with some studies reporting a 50% mortality rate in
patients with acute liver failure who undergo surgery.
In patients with cirrhosis, calculation of the Model for End-Stage Liver Disease score or Child-
Turcotte-Pugh score can predict perioperative morbidity and mortality.
Patients with a history of C difficile should be assessed to determine if a course of
perioperative oral metronidazole or vancomycin would be beneficial.
Neurologic Disease
A documented preoperative neurologic examination with regard to mental status, speech,
cranial nerves, gait, motor function, and sensory function is necessary to allow for
postoperative comparison for any new deficits.
A history of cerebrovascular disease is a risk factor for postoperative cardiac events, stroke,
and death.1
Patients with chronic neurologic diseases (myasthenia gravis, multiple sclerosis, or muscular
dystrophy) should be evaluated by a neurologist preoperatively, and treatment regimens
should be optimized.
The incidence of perioperative stroke is highly variable depending on the type of surgery,
patient age, patient sex, and patient race. The observed incidence of perioperative stroke
during high-risk cardiovascular procedures is as high as 1.9% to 9.7% and approximately 0.5%
to 0.82% during partial hip replacement surgery and 0.45% to 0.66% during open reduction
and internal fixation of the femur.31 The incidence increases with patient age (0.1% to 0.2% for
patients younger than 65 years, 0.5% for patients aged 65 to 74 years, and 1% for patients
older than 75 years.32 Perioperative mortality has been reported to be as high as 18% to
26%.32 If stroke is suspected, emergent imaging studies and neurologic consultation should be
obtained. In general, patients are not candidates for intravenous thrombolytic therapy
postoperatively but may be candidates for intra-arterial thrombolytic procedures.
If cognitive dysfunction occurs postoperatively, the patient must be thoroughly evaluated for
any modifiable causes, including but not limited to infection, pharmacologic causes, hypoxia,
withdrawal, seizure activity, and thyroid disease. Antipsychotic agents, such as haloperidol or
quetiapine, may be administered at the lowest effective dose in patients who are severely
agitated.

Neurologic Disease
Perioperative neurocognitive disorders (PNDs) refer to cognitive impairment during the
perioperative period, including postoperative delirium (including emergence delirium),
delayed neurocognitive recovery (which may be diagnosed as many as 30 days
postoperatively), and postoperative neurocognitive disorder (diagnosed as long as 12
months postoperatively). Some studies use the term postoperative cognitive
dysfunction, which requires a decline on postoperative neurocognitive tests compared
with preoperative tests; therefore postoperative cognitive dysfunction cannot be
established as a clinical diagnosis or via a subjective assessment from the patient, family
members, or staff.
Preoperative risk factors for PND include preexisting cognitive impairment; older patient
age; lower educational achievement; preoperative sleep disruption; excessive alcohol
consumption; psychotropic drug use; and medical comorbidities, such as stroke,
traumatic brain injury, diabetes mellitus, and frailty.
Intraoperative factors that have been implicated in PND include choice of anesthetic
technique (general versus neuraxial), anesthetic depth, hypotension, specific agents
(benzodiazepines, opioids, ketamine, anticholinergic agents), duration of surgery, and
type of surgery. Retrospective data suggest that prolonged surgery duration and the
choice of general anesthesia versus neuraxial anesthesia independently increase the risk
of PND in patients undergoing hip and knee arthroplasty.33,34 However, a prospective
randomized controlled trial reported no considerable difference in the rates of
postoperative cognitive dysfunction in patients who received general versus neuraxial
anesthesia during extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy.35 More recently, a randomized
superiority trial comparing spinal versus general anesthesia in approximately 1,600
patients who underwent hip fracture surgery reported no substantial difference in
mortality, the ability to ambulate after 60 days, or the incidence of delirium between the
two groups.36 Regardless, modifiable risk factors likely exist.
Postoperatively, nonpharmacologic measures, such as frequent reorientation and
reassurance, early ambulation (if possible), and maintenance of sensory input

Traditional laboratory tests include complete blood count, serum electrolyte levels, urine

Substance Abuse and Pain Management
Patients should be assessed for the use of tobacco, alcohol, and illicit substances
preoperatively.
For patients being treated via chronic opioid therapy, the state prescription monitoring registry
may be reviewed to assess patient prescriptions filled for controlled substances.
A toxicology screen should be performed in all patients being treated via daily opioid
medications or in whom illicit drug use is suspected.
In general, patients being treated via chronic opioid therapy (for chronic pain or an opioid use
disorder) should be maintained on their home opioid regimens with the addition of
supplemental pain management strategies (nonpharmacologic adjuncts, nonopioid adjuncts,
regional anesthesia, and/or additional opioid therapy) if possible, with adjustments for
breakthrough pain in the setting of surgery.

Substance Abuse and Pain Management
Patients undergoing chronic opioid therapy (for chronic pain or an opioid use disorder)
pose a considerable challenge with regard to acute pain management in the
perioperative setting. Treatment strategies should aim to provide adequate analgesia,
prevent withdrawal syndrome, and avoid inducing or exacerbating opioid use disorders.
Preoperative discussions between the physician and the patient should include the
anticipated level of pain associated with the planned surgery, various analgesic
modalities that can be implemented, and the probability of additional opioid therapy in
the postoperative period with the goal of returning to the baseline opioid regimen. In
general, preoperative tapering of current opioid regimens (methadone or
buprenorphine) is not recommended. Patients should be maintained on their home
regimens with the addition of nonpharmacologic modalities and nonopioid analgesic
agents if possible, with adjustments for breakthrough pain in the setting of surgery.
Regional anesthesia should be strongly considered in all patients undergoing
orthopaedic procedures, particularly in opioid-tolerant or opioid-dependent patients.
Options include spinal anesthesia, epidural anesthesia (intraoperative and/or
postoperative adjunct), and peripheral nerve blocks with or without continuous
perineural catheters (eg, interscalene, supraclavicular, infraclavicular, sciatic, femoral,
popliteal fossa, adductor canal). Continuous femoral nerve blocks have been shown to
reduce adjuvant analgesic agents, reduce pain during rehabilitation, and promote earlier
knee flexion to 120° after total knee arthroplasty.37
Nonpharmacologic strategies to consider in the perioperative period include
transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation, acupuncture, massage, cognitive-behavior
therapy, music therapy, and hypnosis.38-41 Nonopioid pharmacologic strategies to
consider include acetaminophen, NSAIDs, gabapentinoids (gabapentin and pregabalin),
low-dose intravenous ketamine, and intravenous lidocaine infusion.
Intravenous ketamine has been increasing in popularity as an effective perioperative
adjunct to reduce opioid requirements and decrease overall pain scores in opioid-naïve,
opioid-tolerant, and opioid-dependent patients.42,43 Based on the 2018 Consensus

Anticoagulation Management
Perioperative management strategies must be individualized based on the anticipated risk of
bleeding associated with the procedure and the anticipated risk of thromboembolism while
anticoagulation therapy is withheld.
Vitamin K antagonists (eg, warfarin) should be discontinued 3 to 5 days preoperatively, with
the international normalized ratio measured daily until it is less than or equal to 1.5, and low-
molecular-weight heparin or unfractionated heparin should be initiated at least 1 day after the
discontinuation of vitamin K antagonists.9
Direct oral anticoagulants (eg, dabigatran, rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban) should be
discontinued two to three times their respective half-lives preoperatively in patients with a
normal bleeding risk and four to five times their respective half-lives preoperatively in patients
with a high bleeding risk.9 Earlier cessation should be considered in patients with decreased
renal function (Table 6).

Anticoagulation Management
Conditions considered high risk for thromboembolism include atrial fibrillation with a
CHA2DS2-VASc score higher than or equal to 4, a mechanical prosthetic heart valve, a
newly inserted biologic prosthetic heart valve, mitral valvular repair within the past 3
months, and thrombophilia.9
Malnutrition
Patients with malnutrition have an increased risk for perioperative complications, including
infection, impaired wound healing, pressure ulcers, and longer hospital length of stay. These
patients also may be frail, which is an additional risk factor for perioperative complications.
Preoperative identification of malnutrition and referral to a registered dietician for nutrition
counseling and weight management will prepare patients for a better outcome.
Traditional laboratory studies, such as albumin level, prealbumin level, transferrin level, and
total lymphocyte count, are no longer thought to be reliable indicators of malnutrition.
Currently, malnutrition is defined using established criteria that include weight loss, energy
intake, subcutaneous fat depletion, muscle mass depletion, fluid accumulation, and functional
assessment.45
Tobacco Use
For numerous medical and surgical reasons, smoking cessation should be encouraged
preoperatively. Ideally, patients should be referred to a smoking cessation program 1 to 3
months preoperatively.
Although the precise timing is unknown, patients should cease using tobacco at least 4 weeks
preoperatively.

Tobacco use is associated with impaired wound healing; an increased risk of osteoporosis-
related fractures; nonunion of diaphyseal (humerus, femur, tibia) fractures; and increased
adverse surgical events, including delayed union, nonunion, and reconstructive soft-tissue flap
failure.46-51
Commonly used medications to aid in tobacco cessation include nicotine-replacement
products (lozenges, gum, patches, inhalers, nasal sprays) and non-nicotine medications
(bupropion and varenicline).
Bone Health
Poor bone quality may negatively affect surgical outcomes (eg, periprosthetic fractures,
implant failure, and lack of bony fusion or osseointegration).
Postmenopausal women and men older than 70 years should undergo a bone density
examination within 2 years of a planned orthopaedic procedure involving bony
instrumentation.
Quantitative CT can help determine the bone density of vertebral bodies in the spine of
patients with substantial degenerative disease.
Dual-energy x-ray absorptiometry is more accurate than radiography in evaluating bone
density but may result in falsely elevated values in patients with degenerative disease.
Vitamin D is essential for bone development, skeletal remodeling, and fracture repair.
Currently, adults should have a 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of 20 ng/mL or higher, and many
experts recommended a 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of 30 ng/mL or higher for patients with
osteoporosis.
Diphosphonates do not affect the outcome of arthroplasty. These medications reduce disuse
osteoporosis about the implant.52
Diphosphonates may affect fracture repair. They may be withheld during fracture repair;
however, their half-life is long. Diphosphonates may help prevent implant failure after spinal
fusion.53
Parathyroid hormone may enhance spine fusion.
Infection Prevention
For orthopaedic procedures, the goal is to prevent surgical site infection and periprosthetic
joint infection (PJI).

Dental infection may lead to bacteremia and PJI; therefore, patients should be evaluated
preoperatively with regard to compliance with dental evaluations and cleanings. Patients
should be reminded that after arthroplasty, they will need to be treated via an antibiotic agent
before dental work to help prevent PJI. The length of time from arthroplasty to antibiotic

The mediation regimen of patients with active psoriasis should be adjusted. Psoriatic plaques
may be a nidus for bacteremia and/or surgical site contamination and increase the risk of PJI.
Increasing evidence suggests that skin colonization with Staphylococcus aureus is associated
with surgical site infection.54
Targeted decolonization protocols and universal decolonization protocols have been
proposed. For decolonization, intranasal mupirocin and topical chlorhexidine and povidone
have been used.55,56

Summary
These guidelines and recommendations are merely a framework to aid in clinical
decision making in the perioperative period and should not be interpreted as rigid rules
of practice. Exceptional perioperative care requires individualized risk-benefit analysis of
patient- and procedure-specific risk factors based on current available evidence.
Knowledge of risks allows for more informed discussion between patients and
physicians and more individualized, targeted treatment plans to reduce adverse
perioperative complications.
